groups.title: Normal pancreas
groups.blurb: The reference for everything else: lobules of acini, the ducts that drain them, and the islets scattered among them.

groups.title: Injury and repair
groups.blurb: Benign changes of ducts and acini after injury, which matter mostly because they can be mistaken for precursor lesions.

groups.title: Pancreatitis
groups.blurb: Inflammation of the gland, from mild oedema and fat necrosis to scarring that replaces the acini.

groups.title: Cysts that are not mucinous
groups.blurb: Most pancreatic cysts are not neoplastic; these two are the common ones that carry no mucinous lining.

groups.title: Precursor lesions
groups.blurb: Non-invasive lesions of the duct lining from which ductal adenocarcinoma can arise.

groups.title: Ductal adenocarcinoma by grade
groups.blurb: The common pancreatic cancer, graded by how well it still forms glands, and the scar-like stroma it sits in.

groups.title: Variants of ductal adenocarcinoma
groups.blurb: Less common patterns of the same cancer, some with a different outlook or a different list of look-alikes.

groups.title: How it spreads
groups.blurb: The routes ductal adenocarcinoma takes out of the gland: along nerves, vessels and ducts, to nodes and to the liver.

groups.title: Other tumours (the differential)
groups.blurb: Tumours of the pancreas that are not ductal adenocarcinoma and are told from it by their cells and stroma.

entries.name: Lobule
entries.line: Most of the gland is acinar tissue, with ducts, vessels, a little matrix and scattered islets.

images.caption: Lobules of acini between thin septa, with pale islets. The stain on this slide is bluish, with weak eosin.
images.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Dark acinar tissue fills almost the whole field
Pale islets scattered among the acini
Ducts with collagen walls, thicker as they get larger
entries.remember: The bulk of the gland is acinar, yet most pancreatic tumours are ductal.

features.architecture: Acini and acinar tubules form a joined-up tubular network, not grapes on a stalk; small islets lie among acini, larger ones along the bigger ducts.
features.cells: By volume about 82% acinar cells, 4% duct cells, 4% vessels, 2% endocrine and 8% matrix (the cited measurement is probably from guinea pig).
features.stroma: Stellate cells, 4–7% of parenchymal cells, lie round the bases of acini, small ducts, vessels and islets.

facts.size: The whole gland is 14–25 cm long and about 100 g.
facts.where: The exocrine part is over 95% of the gland by mass.

entries.name: Acini
entries.line: Enzyme-making cells round a tiny lumen: blue at the base, pink at the apex.

images.caption: Acini: pyramidal cells with basal nuclei round small lumina. Eosin is weak on this slide, so the granules look pale.
images.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Cell base stains blue; the apex facing the lumen stains pink
Round nucleus with a nucleolus in the basal half
No mucin anywhere
entries.remember: Blue base, pink granular apex, basal nucleus, no mucin.

features.architecture: Acini and acinar tubules join into a network; classic rounded acini sit at some of its tips.
features.cells: Pyramidal cells about 20 µm across; apical zymogen granules about 1 µm (0.5–1.4 µm).
features.nuclei: Basal, with nucleoli; many cells have two nuclei.
features.mucin: None; the apical cytoplasm holds zymogen granules.

facts.where: Throughout every lobule; acinar cells are about 70% of all pancreatic cells, ductal cells about 18.5%.

mimics.tell: In ADM the cells have lost their granules and form small tubes, usually with fibrosis and inflammation round them.
The carcinoma is a bulky mass of uniform cells in acini or solid sheets, each nucleus with one prominent nucleolus.

entries.name: Centroacinar cells
entries.line: Small pale cells where the acinus meets its ductule: the first cells of the duct system.
glance: Pale cells at the centre of an acinus
Smaller than the acinar cells round them
No granules in their cytoplasm
entries.remember: A pale, granule-free cell inside an acinus is a centroacinar cell.

features.architecture: They sit where an acinus or acinar tubule joins a small ductule, or scattered within an acinar tubule, and form part of the lumen wall.
features.cells: Smaller than acinar cells, with paler cytoplasm, less rough endoplasmic reticulum, no secretory granules, many mitochondria and microvilli on the lumen side.

see.label: See them inside an acinus in 3D

entries.name: Small duct (intralobular)
entries.line: A single layer of low cuboidal cells inside a lobule, with little or no wall: where PanIN begins.

images.caption: A small duct cut lengthwise, one layer of cuboidal cells. Photographed by phase contrast, so the colours are not those of ordinary H&E.
images.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: One even layer of cuboidal to low-columnar cells
No mucin, no crowding of nuclei
Thin collagen wall, or none round the smallest ductules
Pink juice in the lumen
entries.remember: Low, even, mucin-free lining: any mucin in a small duct is abnormal.

features.architecture: A continuous single-layered tube; tight junctions between duct, centroacinar and acinar cells keep the enzymes inside.
features.cells: Cuboidal to low-columnar with amphophilic cytoplasm.
features.stroma: A modest collagen wall; the terminal ductule (intercalated duct) has almost none.

facts.where: Inside the lobules. PanIN arises in these small ducts and ductules.

mimics.tell: PanIN cells are tall and columnar with mucin above a basal nucleus; the normal lining is low and has no mucin.
Reactive ducts have enlarged nuclei with nucleoli and inflammatory cells in and round the lining.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 892

entries.name: Large duct (interlobular)
entries.line: A larger duct in the septum between lobules: one layer of duct cells inside a thick collagen wall.

images.caption: A large duct in a septum with its thick collagen wall; the lining is partly detached.
images.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Single layer of duct cells round a wide lumen
Thick, dense collagen wall
Runs between lobules, not inside one
Larger islets often lie beside it
entries.remember: The thick collagen wall marks a large duct; the lining is still a single mucin-free layer.

features.architecture: A single-layered tube whose collagen wall thins as the ducts branch and narrow.
features.cells: A single layer of cuboidal duct cells.
features.stroma: Conspicuous dense collagen wall, thinner than the main duct’s.

facts.size: The main duct on endoscopic ultrasound measures about 2.4 mm in the head, 1.8 mm in the body and 1.2 mm in the tail.
facts.where: In the septa between lobules, leading to the main duct.

mimics.tell: IPMN fills a main or branch duct with mucinous papillae and is large enough to see by eye or on imaging.

entries.name: Islet of Langerhans
entries.line: A pale, rounded island of small hormone-making cells among the darker acini.

images.caption: A pale islet among darker acini (bluish stain, weak eosin).
images.credit: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: An islet in ordinary H&E colours: pale cells with round nuclei, darker acini round it. The species is not stated on the file page.
images.credit: User:Polarlys, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Paler than the acini round it
Cells smaller than acinar cells
Rounded island, usually 100–150 µm across
entries.remember: A pale island of small uniform cells among dark acini is an islet.

features.architecture: Small islets lie scattered among acini; larger ones lie along the main and interlobular ducts.
features.cells: Smaller and paler than acinar cells. Beta cells 75–80%, alpha about 15%, delta about 5%; alpha and delta cells sit mainly at the edges of beta-cell groups.

facts.size: About 70% are 50–250 µm across, averaging 100–150 µm.
facts.where: Half a million to a million islets, 1–2% of the gland. In the uncinate process islets are PP-rich (54–94% of islet volume).

mimics.tell: A neuroendocrine tumour looks like a giant islet: the same cords of uniform cells along vessels, but forming a mass.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 24, p. 1121

entries.name: Reactive duct
entries.line: A duct responding to inflammation: bigger nuclei and nucleoli, but an orderly lining and no papillae.
glance: Enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli
Neutrophils in and round the lining
Lining stays flat, without papillae
entries.remember: Inflammation in the epithelium plus smooth nuclei with fine chromatin means reactive, not PanIN.

features.architecture: Usually without the papillae or micropapillae that PanIN can show.
features.nuclei: Enlarged, with prominent nucleoli, but smooth outlines and finely dispersed chromatin.
features.stroma: A marked inflammatory infiltrate, especially neutrophils within the epithelium.

facts.where: In inflamed or injured gland; in chronic pancreatitis the duct lining may be atrophic, hyperplastic or squamous.

mimics.tell: PanIN has tall mucinous cells and may be papillary; reactive ducts have inflammation, no papillae, and smooth nuclei with fine chromatin.
Cancer glands have lost the lobular layout, may be incomplete, sit beside muscular arteries, and invade nerves.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 888

entries.name: Acinar-to-ductal metaplasia
entries.line: Acini are replaced by small duct-like tubes, usually with fibrosis and inflammation round them.

images.caption: Obstructive pancreatitis: acini turning into small duct-like tubes with open lumina (arrows, from the source figure).
images.credit: Hosomi K et al. Current Issues in Molecular Biology 2026, doi:10.3390/cimb48060585, figure 1

glance: Small tubes where acini should be
Cells without zymogen granules
Fibrosis and inflammatory cells between the tubes
entries.remember: It is a change of acini inside a lobule, not of a duct, and it can hold mucin like low-grade PanIN.

features.architecture: Progressive replacement of acini by ductular (tubular) structures within a lobule.
features.cells: Cells lose acinar markers and gain ductal ones.
features.mucin: May be present in the cytoplasm, which makes it resemble low-grade PanIN.

facts.where: Inside lobules; common in specimens resected for inflammatory or neoplastic disease.
facts.molecular: Can carry KRAS mutations, but a PanIN may be mutated when the ADM beside it is not.
facts.outlook: Its meaning in humans is unclear and it need not be reported. In mice it is reversible unless mutant Kras and inflammation drive it on to PanIN.

mimics.tell: PanIN lines a duct with tall mucinous cells; ADM is a cluster of small tubes replacing acini within a lobule.

mimics.name: Atypical flat lesion
mimics.tell: Also small intralobular ducts under 0.5 cm, but with cytological atypia and a cellular, whorled stroma.

entries.name: Squamous metaplasia
entries.line: The single-layered duct lining is replaced by mature squamous or transitional epithelium, several layers thick, without atypia.
glance: Several layers of cells where one is expected
Bland, orderly cells
Stays inside the duct
entries.remember: Layered but bland and confined to the duct; malignant squamous nests in the stroma are adenosquamous carcinoma.

features.architecture: Mature stratified squamous or pseudostratified transitional epithelium replacing the cuboidal lining.

facts.where: Ducts, mostly in chronic pancreatitis; beside only about 4% of adenocarcinomas.
facts.outlook: No step from this metaplasia to squamous carcinoma has been shown.

mimics.tell: The carcinoma has infiltrating squamous nests and a glandular component; metaplasia is bland, orderly and inside a duct.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 888

entries.name: Acute interstitial pancreatitis
entries.line: Oedema, mild inflammation and small spots of fat necrosis; the lobules stay intact.
glance: Septa widened by oedema
Small foci of fat necrosis in the fat between lobules
Granular blue deposits where fat has turned to soap
Acini beside the necrosis still intact
entries.remember: Fat necrosis comes first and sets the severity; the acini beside it are preserved.

features.architecture: Tiny fat necroses in the interlobular fat; lobules largely preserved.
features.cells: Acinar cells next to the necrosis stay intact.
features.stroma: Oedema and mild inflammation. Fatty acids freed by lipase bind calcium into insoluble salts that look granular blue.

facts.size: Fat necroses usually under 10 mm; they resolve and leave nothing behind.
facts.who: 90–95% of acute pancreatitis. Biliary disease and alcohol cause about 80%; 10–20 cases per 100,000 a year.
facts.gross: Gland swollen or of normal size, with tiny white spots on its surface and in the fat between lobules.

mimics.tell: The necrotizing form has large confluent fat necrosis reaching beyond the gland, haemorrhage, and dead acini and ducts.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 884, 887

entries.name: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis
entries.line: Large confluent fat necrosis with haemorrhage; acini, ducts and islets in the affected lobules die.

images.caption: Fat necrosis (below) with a rim of inflammation and haemorrhage; viable fat above.
images.credit: Patho, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Coagulative necrosis of pancreatic tissue, congested vessels and an inflammatory infiltrate.
images.credit: Mihoc et al. Biomedicines 2024, doi:10.3390/biomedicines12112627, fig. 12

images.caption: At autopsy: a dark, haemorrhagic gland with yellow-white fat necrosis.
images.credit: Wickramasinghe CU et al. Journal of Medical Case Reports 2023, doi:10.1186/s13256-023-03906-0, fig. 3b

glance: Wide confluent fat necrosis, reaching beyond the gland
Haemorrhage where veins are damaged
Dead acini and ducts in the affected lobules
entries.remember: Fat necrosis dominates; the parenchyma is usually much less necrotic than the fat round it.

features.architecture: Confluent fat necrosis extending into the tissue round the pancreas; parenchymal necrosis usually much less extensive.
features.cells: Acinar and duct tissue necrotic; islets spared unless their lobule is largely necrotic.
features.stroma: Haemorrhage through damaged and thrombosed vessels, veins first; thick-walled arteries resist longer.

facts.size: Necrosis of 2–5 cm can resorb; over 5 cm it often walls off, with granulation tissue by 10–20 days and fibrosis from 20–30 days.
facts.who: 5–10% of acute pancreatitis.
facts.gross: Red-black gland with yellow-white chalky spots; fat necrosis also in omentum, mesentery, even under the skin.
facts.outlook: About 5% of severe cases die in the first week; 40–60% of necrotic debris becomes infected. Repeated necrosis and scarring can lead to chronic pancreatitis.

mimics.tell: The mild form has only oedema and fat necroses under 10 mm, with lobules preserved and no haemorrhage.
Once a fibrous wall fully surrounds old necrosis (after 20–30 days) it is walled-off necrosis.

mimics.name: Two rare patterns
mimics.tell: Necrosis of duct lining with neutrophil plugs, or scattered acinar-cell necrosis (seen with infection), each without fat necrosis.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 887

entries.name: Chronic pancreatitis
entries.line: Scar replaces the acini; ducts dilate and fill with plugs and stones; islets survive for a time in the fibrosis.

images.caption: Fibrosis round a shrunken lobule.
images.credit: Chekmareva et al. Int J Mol Sci 2025, doi:10.3390/ijms262010169, fig. 1A

images.caption: Acini gone; fibrous tissue with vessels and a last group of cells.
images.credit: Chekmareva et al. Int J Mol Sci 2025, doi:10.3390/ijms262010169, fig. 1B

images.caption: An islet left embedded in fibrosis.
images.credit: Chekmareva et al. Int J Mol Sci 2025, doi:10.3390/ijms262010169, fig. 1C

images.caption: Resected head: firm fibrotic gland, dilated duct, stones.
images.credit: D. Desaulniers and B. Têtu, Université Laval, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Dense fibrosis where acini have dropped out
Islets left embedded in scar, sometimes fused and enlarged
Dilated ducts with protein plugs or calcified stones
Chronic inflammatory cells round lobules and ducts
entries.remember: Acini are lost but the lobular outline survives, which separates it from cancer.

features.architecture: Fibrosis, atrophy and dropout of acini, variable duct dilation; chronic inflammation round lobules and ducts.
features.cells: Duct lining atrophic, hyperplastic or squamous. Islets relatively spared, lost in advanced disease.
features.stroma: Collagen laid down by stellate cells driven by TGF-beta and PDGF, the same cells active in cancer.

facts.who: Alcohol is by far the commonest cause; mostly middle-aged men; up to 25% have a genetic basis.
facts.gross: Hard, shrunken gland with an irregular outline, dilated ducts and calcified concretions; duct stones in about half.
facts.molecular: Inherited risk through PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR, CASR, CTRC and CPA1.
facts.outlook: Mortality 50% at 20–25 years; diabetes in 70%; pseudocysts in 10–40%; cancer risk about 12-fold.

mimics.tell: Cancer has lost the lobular layout: incomplete glands, ducts beside muscular arteries, luminal necrosis, invasion of nerves and vessels.
Autoimmune pancreatitis has dense lymphocytes and plasma cells round ducts, storiform fibrosis and obliterated veins, and responds to steroids.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 886, 888–889

entries.name: Autoimmune pancreatitis
entries.line: A steroid-responsive pancreatitis that can pass for cancer: type 1 is rich in plasma cells, type 2 in neutrophils.

images.caption: IgG4-related disease centred on the main duct, one figure in panels: slices with a thickened duct wall (A–C); dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with storiform fibrosis, and IgG4-positive plasma cells in brown (D); a duct and a vein narrowed by inflammation (E, F; elastic and IgG4 stains at right). Small panels.
images.credit: Kanamaru K et al. Clinical Journal of Gastroenterology 2026, doi:10.1007/s12328-026-02315-2, fig. 5

glance: Type 1: dense lymphocytes and plasma cells cuffing ducts
Type 1: swirling (storiform) fibrosis and obliterated veins
Type 2: neutrophils in the duct lining and lumen
entries.remember: It responds to steroids and can masquerade as pancreatic cancer.

features.architecture: Type 1: infiltrate round medium and small ducts compresses them, lining intact. Type 2: neutrophils in and round ducts and acini destroy the lining.
features.cells: Type 1: lymphocytes and IgG4-positive plasma cells. Type 2: neutrophils (the granulocytic epithelial lesion).
features.stroma: Type 1: storiform fibrosis, rich in macrophages and poor in fibroblasts, with obliterative phlebitis.

facts.who: Type 1: mostly elderly men with painless jaundice, dominant in East Asia, part of IgG4-related disease. Type 2: younger, either sex; a third have inflammatory bowel disease.
facts.gross: On imaging, a long irregular narrowing of the main duct with only slight dilation upstream.
facts.outlook: Responds to steroids.

mimics.name: Ductal adenocarcinoma
mimics.tell: Cancer gives a short, severe stricture with marked dilation upstream; autoimmune pancreatitis a long irregular narrowing with little dilation.
Ordinary chronic pancreatitis has duct plugs, stones and plain scarring rather than plasma-cell cuffs, storiform fibrosis and phlebitis.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 888

entries.name: Pseudocyst and walled-off necrosis
entries.line: A collection of enzyme-rich fluid and debris walled in by scar, with no epithelial lining at all.

images.caption: A resected pseudocyst at very low power: the cavity is bounded by fibrous tissue with no epithelial lining; pancreatic lobules beside it (small image; letter from the source figure).
images.credit: Miyata T et al. International Journal of Surgery Case Reports 2026, doi:10.1097/RC9.0000000000000160, fig. 5B

glance: Wall of fibrin, granulation tissue and fibrous tissue
No epithelium on the inner surface
Necrotic or haemorrhagic debris inside
entries.remember: No epithelial lining: any lining means it is not a pseudocyst.

features.architecture: A cavity bounded by fibrin, granulation tissue and fibrous tissue.
features.cells: No epithelial lining.
features.mucin: None; the fluid is rich in amylase, usually from a ruptured duct.
features.stroma: Granulation and fibrous tissue; the pancreas beside it shows pancreatitis.

facts.where: In the gland or, more often, the lesser sac or retroperitoneum; walled-off necrosis mostly outside the gland near the head.
facts.who: About 75% of pancreatic cysts. After acute pancreatitis, often on chronic alcoholic disease, or trauma; in 20–40% of chronic pancreatitis.
facts.gross: The wall can be necrotic and brown-black.
facts.outlook: About 40% resolve by 6 weeks.

mimics.tell: A mucinous cystic neoplasm has a columnar mucinous lining over ovarian-type stroma.
An IPMN is lined by mucinous epithelium and connects with a duct.
A serous cystadenoma is lined by one layer of clear cuboidal cells.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 889–890

entries.name: Serous cystadenoma
entries.line: A sponge of tiny cysts lined by one layer of clear, glycogen-rich cuboidal cells; almost always benign.

images.caption: Small cysts lined by one layer of low cuboidal cells in fibrous stroma.
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: The lining at very high power: cuboidal cells with pale cytoplasm and round central nuclei.
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: The tumour (left) beside normal acini (right).
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Many small cysts, like a sponge
One layer of cuboidal cells with clear cytoplasm
Small, round, central nuclei, all alike
entries.remember: Clear cuboidal cells and watery fluid: no mucin, no ovarian-type stroma.

features.architecture: Microcystic: innumerable millimetre cysts, often round a central scar. A macrocystic form has one or a few large cysts; a solid form exists.
features.cells: A single layer of cuboidal cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm.
features.nuclei: Small, uniform, round, central; no atypia.
features.mucin: None; the fluid is watery and straw-coloured.

facts.where: Usually the tail (Robbins) or body and tail (Beger); no connection with the ducts.
facts.size: Cysts 1–3 mm; the mass averages 4–6 cm at diagnosis and grows about 0.6 cm a year.
facts.who: About 25% of cystic neoplasms; two-thirds or more are women; sixth to seventh decade.
facts.molecular: VHL inactivation; several lesions suggest von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. No KRAS, RNF43 or TP53 mutations.
facts.outlook: Almost always benign; without symptoms, surgery is usually not needed.

mimics.tell: MCN has tall mucinous cells over ovarian-type stroma and thick mucin; the macrocystic serous form can look like it on imaging.
IPMN is mucinous, papillary and connected with a duct.
The solid serous form can pass for a neuroendocrine tumour, which has nests of cells with salt-and-pepper nuclei.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 890

entries.name: Low-grade PanIN
entries.aka: pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia; formerly PanIN-1A, 1B and 2
entries.line: Tall mucin-filled cells replace the low lining of a small duct; too small to see by eye.

images.caption: Flat lining of tall columnar cells with mucin above basal nuclei (formerly PanIN-1A).
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 3a

images.caption: Papillary folds, crowded and stratified nuclei (formerly PanIN-2).
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 4a

images.caption: In context: one small duct with a papillary mucinous lining, among normal acini.
images.credit: Hackeng WM et al. Diagn Pathol 2016, doi:10.1186/s13000-016-0497-z, fig. 2a

glance: Tall columnar cells with pale mucin above the nucleus
Nuclei small and basal, or crowded and stacked in former PanIN-2
Flat, or folded into small papillae
entries.remember: Mucin in a small duct means PanIN; grade it by the nuclei.

features.architecture: Flat (former 1A), or papillary, micropapillary or basally pseudostratified (1B and 2).
features.cells: Tall columnar, gastric-foveolar in type.
features.nuclei: 1A and 1B: small, round to oval, basal. Former PanIN-2: some loss of polarity, crowding, enlargement, pseudostratification, darker staining.
features.mitoses: None in former PanIN-1; rare, never at the lumen and never atypical, in former PanIN-2.
features.mucin: Abundant above the nucleus; MUC5AC, MUC1 and MUC4 present, MUC2 usually absent.

facts.where: Small ducts, more often in the head than the tail.
facts.size: Microscopic, usually under 0.5 cm; invisible on imaging.
facts.who: In 82% of pancreata with ductal adenocarcinoma, 60% with chronic pancreatitis and 16% of normal ones; sexes equal.
facts.molecular: KRAS mutated in over 90%; telomere shortening almost universal, even in PanIN-1A; CDKN2A loss follows.
facts.outlook: Common and of no proven clinical significance; at a resection margin it does not alter survival.

mimics.tell: Reactive ducts have inflammation in the lining, no papillae and no mucin cap; nuclei enlarged but smooth, with fine chromatin.
ADM is small tubes replacing acini within a lobule, not a lining change in a duct; it too can hold mucin.
IPMN is 1 cm or more and visible by eye; between 0.5 and 1 cm, long finger-like papillae, intestinal or oncocytic cells or GNAS mutation favour IPMN.
High grade has lost polarity throughout, with budding, cribriform growth or luminal necrosis.

entries.name: High-grade PanIN
entries.line: Cells that look like carcinoma but remain inside the duct: polarity lost, clusters budding into the lumen.

images.caption: Papillae with crowded nuclei that have lost their polarity; a cluster of cells buds into the lumen (formerly PanIN-3).
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 4b

glance: Nuclei at every level of the lining, not lined up at the base
Small clusters of cells budding into the lumen
Cribriform spaces or debris in the lumen
Large nucleoli
entries.remember: It looks like cancer cell by cell, but nothing has crossed the basement membrane.

features.architecture: Usually papillary or micropapillary, rarely flat; true cribriform growth, budding and luminal necrosis.
features.cells: Dystrophic goblet cells: nucleus towards the lumen, mucin towards the basement membrane.
features.nuclei: Polarity lost, irregular outlines, prominent (macro) nucleoli.
features.mucin: Still present, as in the dystrophic goblet cells.

facts.where: Small ducts, almost only in glands that also hold invasive carcinoma.
facts.molecular: TP53, SMAD4 and BRCA2 inactivation are placed at this stage, though SMAD4 loss may come only after invasion.
facts.outlook: Found on its own, it raises suspicion of invasive cancer elsewhere in the gland.

mimics.tell: Invasive cancer lies right beside the duct and the atypical lining stops abruptly against normal lining; SMAD4 or TP53 stains and step sections help.
Tumour cells can replace the endothelium of a vein and line it like a duct.
Low grade keeps most nuclei towards the base and has no budding, cribriform growth or necrosis.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 892

entries.name: IPMN
entries.line: Mucin-making papillae growing inside the main duct or its branches, large enough to see by eye.

images.caption: Low grade: tall, thick papillae of mucinous columnar cells with bland nuclei.
images.credit: Chen et al. Diagnostics 2023, doi:10.3390/diagnostics13010065, fig. 4A

images.caption: High grade: branching papillae, stratified nuclei, less mucin.
images.credit: Chen et al. Diagnostics 2023, doi:10.3390/diagnostics13010065, fig. 4B

images.caption: Gastric type: short papillae of foveolar cells.
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 5a

images.caption: Intestinal type: long finger-like papillae.
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 5c

images.caption: Pancreatobiliary type: complex papillae, atypical nuclei.
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 5e

images.caption: Resected pancreas: dilated main duct with tumour (arrowheads) and branch-duct cysts (arrows and letter from the source figure).
images.credit: Shibata H et al. Clin J Gastroenterol 2017, doi:10.1007/s12328-017-0728-1

glance: Papillae of mucinous columnar cells projecting into a dilated duct
Gastric type: mucin cap, small basal nuclei
Intestinal type: long fingers, cigar-shaped stacked nuclei, goblet cells
Ordinary stroma beneath, never ovarian-type
entries.remember: Inside a duct, papillary, mucinous and without ovarian-type stroma.

features.architecture: Papillae in a dilated main duct, or a grape-like cluster of cysts on a branch duct. High grade: irregular papillae and cribriform growth.
features.cells: Gastric type foveolar-like, mostly branch ducts and low grade. Intestinal type like a villous adenoma. Pancreatobiliary type mucin-poor, mostly high grade.
features.nuclei: Low grade: one layer of small uniform nuclei. High grade: polarity lost, dark and pleomorphic.
features.mucin: Abundant, thick and tenacious; MUC5AC in all types, MUC2 in intestinal, MUC1 in pancreatobiliary.

facts.where: Mostly the head and uncinate process; main duct, branch ducts or both. 10–40% are multifocal.
facts.size: Usually 1 cm or more. Main duct over 5 mm; branch-duct cysts over 10 mm.
facts.who: Usually found in the mid-60s; main-duct type more often in men.
facts.gross: Main duct diffusely dilated with long finger-like papillae and thick mucin; a gaping papilla may extrude mucus.
facts.molecular: KRAS and GNAS each mutated in 50–80%, RNF43 in 14–75%; TP53 in high grade; SMAD4 usually only with invasion.
facts.outlook: Invasive carcinoma in 43.6% of main-duct and 16.6% of branch-duct lesions. Five-year survival after resection 94% for high grade, 31% once invasive.

mimics.tell: MCN does not involve the ducts and has ovarian-type stroma beneath its lining; it has no GNAS mutation.
PanIN is under 0.5 cm, in small ducts, and invisible by eye.
The oncocytic neoplasm has intensely pink cells in several layers with punched-out spaces and no KRAS or GNAS mutation.
Invasive cancer spreading along a duct can imitate it; look for invasive carcinoma beside the duct and an abrupt edge.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 891

entries.name: Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm
entries.line: Branching papillae of intensely pink cells inside a duct, now a separate entity from IPMN.

images.caption: Branching papillae of pink (oncocytic) cells filling a dilated duct. Low power, small image.
images.credit: Xiang Y et al. Front Med 2025, doi:10.3389/fmed.2025.1650931, fig. 4A

glance: Branching papillae, the lining 1–5 cells thick
Abundant pink granular cytoplasm
Round punched-out spaces within the lining
One prominent, off-centre nucleolus
entries.remember: Pink cells and punched-out spaces: it looks high grade yet seldom invades.

features.architecture: Arborizing papillae lined by 1–5 layers of cuboidal cells, with punched-out spaces in the epithelium.
features.cells: Abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, packed with mitochondria.
features.nuclei: Large, with a single prominent eccentric nucleolus.

facts.where: About two-thirds in the head.
facts.who: Men and women equally; about half have no symptoms.
facts.molecular: No KRAS or GNAS mutation; PRKACA or PRKACB gene fusions; MUC5AC, MUC6 and HepPar-1 positive.
facts.outlook: Excellent; invasive carcinoma is uncommon, and tangential cuts can imitate invasion.

mimics.tell: IPMN cells are mucinous rather than pink and granular, and carry KRAS or GNAS mutations.

entries.name: Mucinous cystic neoplasm
entries.line: A mucin-filled cyst lined by columnar cells over a dense, cellular ovarian-type stroma; no connection with the ducts.

images.caption: Columnar mucinous lining over dense ovarian-type stroma of spindle cells.
images.credit: Distler et al. Biomed Res Int 2014, doi:10.1155/2014/474905, fig. 6b

images.caption: Low power: normal pancreas, fibrous capsule, stroma and cysts.
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Columnar mucinous cells lining a cyst
Densely packed spindle cells directly beneath the lining
Stretches of flat or missing lining are common
entries.remember: Ovarian-type stroma defines MCN; IPMN never has it.

features.architecture: A well-demarcated cyst, multilocular or cyst-within-cyst, behind a fibrous pseudocapsule. Papillae or a mural nodule suggest high grade or invasion.
features.cells: From flat or cuboidal with little mucin to tall columnar; low- and high-grade areas coexist; lining often denuded.
features.mucin: Abundant above the nucleus in the tall cells; mucin-rich lining is more often linked with high grade or invasion.
features.stroma: Ovarian-type spindle-cell stroma, required for diagnosis but sometimes focal or masked by fibrosis; oestrogen and progesterone receptors; luteinised cells inhibin-positive.

facts.where: Over 90% in the body or tail; solitary; no, or very rare, communication with the ducts.
facts.size: Median 3.5–5 cm (range 0.5–20 cm; up to 35 cm in one chapter).
facts.who: Almost only women (10–20 to 1), mean age about 45; about ten years older when invasive.
facts.gross: Round, smooth inner surface, thick wall often calcified, tenacious mucin.
facts.molecular: KRAS (up to 100% when high grade or invasive), RNF43; TP53 and CDKN2A in about half of those; no GNAS mutation.
facts.outlook: Resection of a non-invasive MCN is curative. Invasive carcinoma in 6–25% (up to a third in Robbins).

mimics.tell: IPMN involves a duct and has no ovarian-type stroma; GNAS mutation occurs in IPMN, not MCN.
A pseudocyst has no epithelial lining at all, only granulation and fibrous tissue.
Serous cysts are lined by clear cuboidal cells and hold watery fluid, without mucin or ovarian-type stroma.

mimics.name: Simple mucinous cyst
mimics.tell: A flat gastric-type lining with at most minimal atypia and no ovarian-type stroma; benign.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 891

entries.name: Ductal adenocarcinoma, well differentiated
entries.line: Well-formed glands that closely resemble normal ducts, but scattered without order through scar-like stroma.

images.caption: Well-formed glands with open lumina in desmoplastic stroma. The uploader does not state a grade; chosen for its well-formed glands.
images.credit: KGH, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Complete, well-formed glands
Fairly uniform nuclei
Glands placed haphazardly, the lobular pattern gone
A gland lying next to a muscular artery
entries.remember: The cells can look bland: it is the position of the glands, not their nuclei, that gives it away.

features.architecture: Haphazard glands and duct-like structures; lobular layout lost; some glands incomplete; glands beside muscular arteries.
features.cells: Cuboidal or columnar, often with mucin in the cytoplasm.
features.nuclei: Relatively uniform; can be quite bland.
features.mitoses: Fewer than in moderately differentiated tumours.
features.mucin: Present: the cells form glands and secrete mucin.

facts.where: About 60% of ductal adenocarcinomas arise in the head, 15% in the body, 5% in the tail; 20% are diffuse.
facts.who: The exception: most ductal adenocarcinomas are moderately to poorly differentiated. About 80% of cases occur at ages 60–80.
facts.gross: A hard, grey-white, ill-defined mass in the soft yellow gland.
facts.molecular: KRAS in 90–95%, CDKN2A in about 95%, TP53 in 70–75%, SMAD4 in about 55%. Keratins 7 and 19, CEA, mesothelin and MUC1 are used as markers.
facts.outlook: The tumour is graded by its worst area, and grade drives prognosis.

mimics.tell: Reactive glands keep the lobular arrangement; cancer shows incomplete glands, glands beside muscular arteries, luminal necrosis and invasion of nerves and vessels.
A reactive duct sits where a duct belongs, with inflammation in its lining.

mimics.name: Large-duct pattern
mimics.tell: Dilated, irregular mucinous glands can pass for a cystic neoplasm; they dissect through desmoplastic stroma without lobular order.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 892–894

entries.name: Ductal adenocarcinoma, moderately differentiated
entries.line: The usual picture: poorly formed glands of varied cells deep in dense stroma.

images.caption: Irregular glands and cribriform nests of atypical cells in desmoplastic stroma. Grade not stated by the uploader.
images.credit: KGH, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Irregular, crowded glands of atypical cells with debris in the lumen. The source does not state the grade.
images.credit: Singh et al. PLoS One 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0150338

glance: Poorly formed or abortive glands
Cells and nuclei vary in size and shape
Much of the field is fibrous stroma
entries.remember: More variation between cells and more mitoses than a well-differentiated tumour, but still making glands.

features.architecture: Abortive tubules or cell clusters with a deeply infiltrative pattern.
features.cells: Pleomorphic cuboidal to columnar cells.
features.nuclei: More variation than in well-differentiated tumours.
features.stroma: Dense desmoplastic fibrosis; much of a biopsy may be non-neoplastic tissue.

facts.who: With poorly differentiated tumours, the usual form of ductal adenocarcinoma.
facts.molecular: KRAS in 90–95%, CDKN2A in about 95%, TP53 in 70–75%, SMAD4 in about 55%. Keratins 7 and 19, CEA, mesothelin and MUC1 are used as markers.
facts.outlook: Overall five-year survival about 10% or less; 15–25% after resection; fewer than 20% are resectable at diagnosis.

mimics.tell: Well-differentiated tumours form complete glands with fairly uniform nuclei.
Poorly differentiated tumours form few or no glands and grow as sheets or single cells.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 892–894

entries.name: Ductal adenocarcinoma, poorly differentiated
entries.line: Few or no glands: solid sheets and single cells, from small and scant to large and bizarre.

images.caption: Poorly differentiated malignant cells, with few glands, in desmoplastic stroma.
images.credit: Aloraini et al. Cureus 2023, doi:10.7759/cureus.48642, fig. 6

images.caption: Another area of a gland-forming tumour: cords and single cells with only occasional lumina. A tumour is graded by its worst area.
images.credit: KGH, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Solid sheets or single infiltrating cells
Glands absent or barely formed
Some large bizarre cells with abundant pink cytoplasm
entries.remember: No glands, or hardly any: sheets and single cells.

features.architecture: No glands or only poorly formed ones; solid sheets and single cells.
features.cells: From small with scant cytoplasm to large and bizarre with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.

facts.molecular: KRAS in 90–95%, CDKN2A in about 95%, TP53 in 70–75%, SMAD4 in about 55%. Keratins 7 and 19, CEA, mesothelin and MUC1 are used as markers.
facts.outlook: Worse than well or moderately differentiated tumours.

mimics.tell: Undifferentiated carcinoma is a separate category of spindled or bizarre cells with no line of differentiation at all.
Neuroendocrine carcinoma also grows in sheets, with geographic necrosis; a mixed tumour needs over 30% of each component.
Moderately differentiated tumours still form recognisable, if abortive, glands.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 892–893

entries.name: Desmoplastic stroma
entries.line: The dense collagen scar that surrounds the glands of ductal adenocarcinoma and makes the tumour hard.

images.caption: Loose, moderate and dense desmoplastic stroma, side by side.
images.credit: Wang et al. Oncotarget 2016, doi:10.18632/oncotarget.6770

images.caption: Malignant glands in pale desmoplastic stroma.
images.credit: Aloraini et al. Cureus 2023, doi:10.7759/cureus.48642, fig. 3

images.caption: To the eye: a firm, white, ill-defined tumour (T) in the head, beside pancreas (P) and duodenum (D). Small image.
images.credit: Hackeng WM et al. Diagn Pathol 2016, doi:10.1186/s13000-016-0497-z, fig. 1a

glance: Broad bands of dense pink collagen
Fibroblasts (activated stellate cells) between the fibres
Glands can be sparse within it
entries.remember: The stroma can so outweigh the glands that a small biopsy misses the cancer.

features.architecture: Abundant dense collagen round the glands, which may be few.
features.cells: Activated stellate cells (cancer-associated fibroblasts) make the collagen; immune cells, vessels and nerves lie within it.
features.stroma: Poorly vascularised and under high pressure, which may hinder chemotherapy.

facts.gross: Accounts for the firm, sclerotic feel of the tumour.
facts.outlook: A florid stroma can hide the glands in small samples, so extensive sampling is needed before cancer is excluded.

mimics.tell: Scar of chronic pancreatitis keeps the outline of lobules and holds residual islets and orderly ducts, not haphazard glands.
Medullary carcinoma is the contrast: scant fibrous stroma and many lymphocytes.
Acinar cell carcinoma has no prominent desmoplastic stroma.

entries.name: Adenosquamous carcinoma
entries.line: Two cancers in one: ordinary glands with mucin, and nests of malignant squamous cells.

images.caption: Gland-forming and solid squamous areas in one tumour. Low contrast; the squamous part is subtle here.
images.credit: Paramythiotis D et al. J Med Case Rep 2022, doi:10.1186/s13256-022-03610-5, fig. 2a

glance: Glands with mucin in one area
Solid nests of polygonal cells with dense pink cytoplasm in another
Sharp cell borders and bridges between squamous cells
Keratin in some tumours
entries.remember: Find both parts: glands and squamous nests. With no glands, think of a metastasis.

features.architecture: Biphasic: glandular and squamous areas apart or closely mixed.
features.cells: Squamous: polygonal, abundant opaque eosinophilic cytoplasm, distinct borders, intercellular bridges, with or without keratin. Glandular: as ordinary ductal adenocarcinoma.

facts.where: Head 17, tail 9, body 4 in a series of 25 (some in more than one part).
facts.who: 1–4% of exocrine pancreatic cancers; mean age 65; more men than women in that series.
facts.gross: Infiltrative, firm, yellow-white to grey, with softened or liquefied areas.
facts.molecular: KRAS codon 12 mutated in over half. CK5/6 marks the squamous part, CK7 the glands.
facts.outlook: Worse than ordinary ductal adenocarcinoma: mean survival under 6 months in one series. Some respond to platinum.

mimics.tell: Metaplasia is bland, orderly and inside a duct; the carcinoma infiltrates as nests and comes with malignant glands.

mimics.name: Metastatic squamous carcinoma
mimics.tell: If no glandular component is found, a squamous carcinoma from another organ must be considered.

mimics.name: The 30% rule
mimics.tell: Beger asks for at least 30% squamous; Kardon calls that arbitrary and accepts any definite malignant squamous differentiation.

entries.name: Colloid carcinoma
entries.line: Pools of mucin push through the stroma, with strips and clusters of tumour cells floating in them.

images.caption: Pools of pale mucin with strips of tumour cells floating in them (letter and arrow from the source figure).
images.credit: Orcutt ST et al. Case Rep Pancreat Cancer 2016, doi:10.1089/crpc.2016.0006, fig. 2A

glance: Large lakes of pale mucin in the stroma
Tumour cells floating in the mucin or lining its edge
entries.remember: The cells must be in the mucin: spilt mucin from a ruptured cyst is not colloid carcinoma.

features.architecture: Mucin pools dissecting the stroma; neoplastic epithelium lines the pools or floats within them.

facts.who: About 2% of resected pancreatic neoplasms in one large series.
facts.molecular: Arises from intestinal-type IPMN: MUC2 and CDX2 positive, GNAS often mutated.
facts.outlook: Better than ordinary ductal adenocarcinoma: median survival 107 against 20 months when arising from IPMN.

mimics.name: Ruptured mucinous cyst
mimics.tell: Mucin spilt into the stroma without malignant cells in it should not be called invasive.
Intestinal-type IPMN is its usual source; the carcinoma is the mucin, with cells, beyond the duct.
Signet-ring cells hold their mucin inside the cell and infiltrate singly, without mucin lakes.

entries.name: Undifferentiated carcinoma
entries.aka: anaplastic; the spindle-cell pattern some call sarcomatoid
entries.line: Spindled or large bizarre cells that hold together poorly and show no line of differentiation.

images.caption: Sheets of large, bizarre tumour cells, some with several nuclei, and haemorrhage (small image; letter from the source figure).
images.credit: Olayinka O et al. Cureus 2021, doi:10.7759/cureus.14988, fig. 1B

glance: Loose sheets of large bizarre cells
Or bundles of spindle cells
No glands; cells falling apart from one another
entries.remember: No glands, no cohesion: grade it by this part even when ordinary glands lie beside it.

features.architecture: Loosely cohesive sheets; often an ordinary lower-grade gland-forming component beside it.
features.cells: Predominantly spindled, or large and bizarre; less cohesive than ordinary ductal adenocarcinoma (E-cadherin lost); some rhabdoid.
features.nuclei: Bizarre, with prominent nucleoli; cells with several nuclei occur.

facts.outlook: Fast growing and often widely metastatic; mean survival under one year.

mimics.tell: There the giant cells are bland, non-neoplastic and CD68-positive; here the large bizarre cells are the tumour.
A poorly differentiated tumour still follows a ductal line, with poor glands, sheets or single cells; this has no line of differentiation.

mimics.name: “Sarcomatoid carcinoma”
mimics.tell: The books read (Beger, Robbins, Kleeff) do not use this term for the pancreas; they describe undifferentiated carcinoma of spindled cells.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells
entries.line: Malignant spindled or bizarre cells mixed with many large giant cells that are not themselves tumour.

images.caption: Large cells with many nuclei (arrowheads, from the source figure) among smaller tumour cells.
images.credit: Chan W et al. J Med Case Rep 2023, doi:10.1186/s13256-023-04213-4, fig. 4C

glance: Many giant cells, each with numerous nuclei
Spindled or bizarre single-nucleus cells between them
entries.remember: The giant cells are bystanders; the malignant cells are the ones in between.

features.architecture: Numerous multinucleated giant cells scattered through an undifferentiated carcinoma.
features.cells: Giant cells: non-neoplastic, histiocytic (CD68-positive). Cells between them: malignant, spindled or bizarre, often keratin-positive.

facts.outlook: Poor: mean survival under one year.

mimics.tell: Without the osteoclast-like giant cells; its giant forms are malignant, with bizarre nuclei.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Signet-ring cell carcinoma
entries.line: Single cells infiltrating the stroma, each swollen with mucin that pushes its nucleus to one side.

images.caption: Single cells, each with a mucin vacuole pushing the nucleus to the edge (arrow from the source figure).
images.credit: Campbell DJ et al. J Pancreat Cancer 2021, doi:10.1089/pancan.2020.0013, fig. 4

glance: Single cells, not glands or sheets
A droplet of mucin filling each cell
Nucleus indented and pushed to the edge
entries.remember: Before calling it pancreatic, exclude a metastasis from stomach or breast.

features.architecture: Single infiltrating cells rather than glands or sheets.
features.cells: Mucin within the cytoplasm.
features.nuclei: Indented and displaced by the mucin.

facts.who: Rare; the sources read give no frequency.

mimics.name: Metastatic diffuse gastric or lobular breast carcinoma
mimics.tell: They look the same, so a metastasis must be considered before a pancreatic primary is accepted.
Colloid carcinoma has mucin outside the cells, in lakes, with cells floating in it.

entries.name: Medullary carcinoma
entries.line: Sheets of poorly differentiated cells with a pushing edge, many lymphocytes and little fibrous stroma.

images.caption: Sheets of poorly differentiated cells with a pushing edge and lymphocytes (small image; arrows from the source figure).
images.credit: Ohtsubo K et al. Front Oncol 2025, doi:10.3389/fonc.2025.1551038, fig. 2B

glance: Sheets of large cells with borders that run together
Many lymphocytes in and round the tumour
A pushing, rounded edge; hardly any scar
entries.remember: Poorly differentiated yet with a good outlook, and often mismatch-repair deficient.

features.architecture: Syncytial growth with pushing, non-infiltrating borders.
features.cells: Poorly differentiated epithelioid cells.
features.stroma: Scant fibrous stroma; a brisk lymphocytic infiltrate in and round the tumour.

facts.molecular: More often microsatellite unstable (mismatch-repair deficient); possible Lynch syndrome.
facts.outlook: Good despite poor differentiation; PD-1 inhibitors may work.

mimics.tell: Ordinary poorly differentiated carcinoma infiltrates, in dense desmoplastic stroma, without the lymphocytes or the pushing edge.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Hepatoid carcinoma
entries.line: Polygonal pink cells that look like liver cancer but arise in the pancreas.

images.caption: Polygonal cells with abundant pink cytoplasm and round nuclei, like liver cells.
images.credit: Tomino T et al. Surg Case Rep 2019, doi:10.1186/s40792-019-0723-5, fig. 4

glance: Polygonal cells
Abundant pink cytoplasm, like liver cells
entries.remember: Exclude a metastasis from the liver first.

features.cells: Polygonal and eosinophilic, resembling hepatocellular carcinoma.

facts.molecular: May stain for hepatocyte antigen (Hep-Par) and alpha-fetoprotein.

mimics.name: Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma
mimics.tell: It looks the same; a liver primary must be excluded before a pancreatic one is diagnosed.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Perineural invasion
entries.line: Malignant glands growing along and round a nerve: present in practically every ductal adenocarcinoma.

images.caption: Malignant glands round a nerve.
images.credit: KGH, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: A nerve: a pale bundle of wavy fibres
Glands wrapped round it or inside its sheath
entries.remember: A gland in or round a nerve is cancer, not a reactive duct.

features.architecture: Tumour tracks along and round nerves, within the pancreas and beyond it.

facts.who: Practically all ductal adenocarcinomas; 80% of adenosquamous carcinomas in one series.
facts.outlook: May explain the pain (about 70% of patients) and gives the tumour a path out of the gland.

mimics.tell: Reactive glands of chronic pancreatitis do not invade nerves; finding a gland there settles it.

entries.name: Vascular invasion
entries.line: Tumour inside a vein, often not as a plug but as a lining that makes the vein look like a duct.

images.caption: Round plugs of tumour cells inside dilated lymphatic vessels (labels from the source figure).
images.credit: Satala CB et al. Surg J (N Y) 2021, doi:10.1055/s-0041-1728651, fig. 2A-B

glance: A vessel lined by tumour cells in place of endothelium
Cells flattened along the wall, like a duct lining
Often no tumour plug in the lumen
entries.remember: In veins the cells flatten along the wall and imitate a duct or PanIN.

features.architecture: Cells flatten and grow along the endothelial surface rather than forming a tumour thrombus.

facts.who: Practically all ductal adenocarcinomas; lymphatic and large-vessel invasion are common.
facts.outlook: Leads to widespread dissemination, especially to the liver.

mimics.tell: PanIN lines a duct; here the same picture is tumour that has replaced the endothelium of a vein.
Both are tumour lining a pre-existing tube: one a duct, the other a vein.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Cancerization of ducts
entries.line: Invasive carcinoma grows back along a pre-existing duct and replaces its lining, imitating high-grade PanIN.
glance: Highly atypical lining that stops abruptly against normal lining
Invasive glands right beside the duct
entries.remember: An abrupt front inside one duct, with invasive cancer next door, means cancerization.

features.architecture: Carcinoma extends along ducts and ductules; an abrupt transition from highly atypical to normal epithelium within the same duct.

facts.who: Reported in as many as 70% of resections for invasive pancreatic cancer.
facts.molecular: SMAD4 or TP53 immunostains may help; step sections show its link with the invasive tumour.
facts.outlook: At a resection margin it may change outcome, whereas PanIN of any grade there does not.

mimics.tell: Without invasive carcinoma beside the duct or an abrupt front against normal lining, high-grade PanIN is favoured.
Spread along larger ducts can imitate IPMN.
Tumour lining a vein gives the same picture: cells flattened along the wall of a pre-existing tube.

entries.name: Lymph node metastasis
entries.line: Tumour deposits in the nodes round the pancreas; at least 12 nodes are needed to stage a resection.

images.caption: A lymph node: tumour cells and glands replace the lymphoid tissue inside the capsule (label from the source figure).
images.credit: Satala CB et al. Surg J (N Y) 2021, doi:10.1055/s-0041-1728651, fig. 2C

glance: Lymphoid tissue of the node
Glands or sheets of tumour cells within it
entries.remember: Count the nodes: staging needs at least 12.

features.cells: The deposit can be less differentiated than the primary; one nodal deposit of an adenosquamous carcinoma was anaplastic.

facts.where: Peripancreatic, gastric, mesenteric, omental and portohepatic nodes. Para-aortic nodes in 16–26% of head and 13–17% of body and tail cancers.
facts.outlook: In invasive MCN nodes are involved in only up to a third, one reason it does better.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Liver metastasis
entries.line: The liver is the main distant site, reached through the veins the tumour invades.

images.caption: Cut surface of a liver with many pale deposits from a pancreatic cancer.
images.credit: Haymanj, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Liver tissue
A deposit of malignant glands with its own fibrous stroma
entries.remember: Distant spread goes chiefly to the liver, then the lungs.

facts.where: Liver and lungs are the main distant sites.
facts.who: 40–50% of patients have metastases at diagnosis; body and tail tumours more often (69% and 84%) than head tumours (42%).
facts.outlook: Five-year survival 3% with distant disease, against 39% when localized.

mimics.tell: The reverse problem: a hepatoid tumour in the pancreas may itself be a metastasis from the liver.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 894

entries.name: Neuroendocrine tumour
entries.line: Nests and ribbons of uniform cells with speckled nuclei, between fine capillaries: like a giant islet.

images.caption: Nests and ribbons of uniform cells with round nuclei, among thin-walled vessels.
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Nuclei at very high power: finely speckled (“salt and pepper”) chromatin.
images.credit: Mikael Häggström, M.D., via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Nests and ribbons of uniform cells
Round nuclei with speckled, salt-and-pepper chromatin
Thin capillaries between the nests
entries.remember: Uniform cells, salt-and-pepper nuclei, a fine capillary stroma.

features.architecture: Solid nests and trabeculae (ribbons).
features.cells: Uniform, with granular, slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm.
features.nuclei: Round to oval; coarsely granular chromatin; inconspicuous nucleoli.
features.mitoses: Counted, with the Ki-67 index, to set the grade (G1 to G3).
features.stroma: Capillary or fibrocapillary; amyloid in many insulinomas.

facts.where: Anywhere in the pancreas or the tissue round it.
facts.size: 0.5–20 cm; insulinomas usually under 2 cm, non-functioning tumours larger.
facts.who: About 2% of pancreatic neoplasms (15–20% of one centre’s resections). Under 40% are functioning; 30–70% of MEN1 patients develop them.
facts.gross: Small ones well circumscribed, whitish-tan to yellow; larger ones multinodular, sometimes cystic.
facts.molecular: Synaptophysin and chromogranin positive. ATRX or DAXX mutated in nearly half; MEN1, PTEN and TSC2 also altered.
facts.outlook: About 90% of insulinomas are benign; 60–90% of the others are malignant, judged by metastasis and invasion, not by how the cells look.

mimics.tell: Acinar cell carcinoma has one prominent nucleolus per nucleus and stains for trypsin and chymotrypsin; up to a third show patchy chromogranin.
The solid pseudopapillary neoplasm has poorly cohesive cells with grooved nuclei and nuclear beta-catenin; LEF1 marks it, INSM1 the neuroendocrine tumour.
The carcinoma grows in sheets with geographic necrosis and marked pleomorphism; Ki-67 mostly over 50%.
An islet is 50–250 µm; the tumour is the same pattern as a mass.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 24, p. 1121

entries.name: Neuroendocrine carcinoma
entries.line: A poorly differentiated neuroendocrine cancer: sheets of pleomorphic cells with wide areas of necrosis.
glance: Solid sheets, without nests or ribbons
Map-like areas of necrosis
Large, varied nuclei filling most of each cell
entries.remember: Not a high-grade version of the tumour: a different disease, with the genetics of ductal adenocarcinoma.

features.architecture: Diffuse or solid sheets with geographic necrosis and unclear borders.
features.nuclei: Large-cell type: marked pleomorphism, enlarged nuclei, high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.
features.mitoses: Numerous; mitotic count and Ki-67 both above the 20 threshold, Ki-67 mostly over 50%.

facts.molecular: Shares the genetic background of ductal adenocarcinoma, not of neuroendocrine tumours.
facts.outlook: Aggressive.

mimics.tell: The tumour keeps nests and ribbons of uniform cells with salt-and-pepper nuclei and little necrosis.
Both grow in sheets. A mixed neuroendocrine and ductal tumour needs over 30% of each component.

entries.name: Acinar cell carcinoma
entries.line: Uniform cells with granular cytoplasm and one prominent nucleolus, in acini or solid sheets, with little stroma.

images.caption: Sheets and small acini of cells with granular cytoplasm; each nucleus with one prominent nucleolus.
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Small acini or solid sheets of similar cells
Granular cytoplasm
One prominent nucleolus in each nucleus
Hardly any fibrous stroma
entries.remember: One prominent nucleolus, granular cytoplasm, and no desmoplastic stroma.

features.architecture: Acini or solid sheets.
features.cells: Monomorphic, with granular cytoplasm (zymogen granules, PAS-diastase positive).
features.nuclei: Large, with a single prominent nucleolus.

facts.who: Under 2% of resected pancreatic neoplasms.
facts.gross: Well circumscribed, bulky, fleshy, often haemorrhagic.
facts.molecular: Trypsin, chymotrypsin and BCL-10 positive.
facts.outlook: Better than ductal adenocarcinoma of the same stage: 25–50% five-year survival. About 15% develop fat necrosis at distant sites from released lipase.

mimics.tell: Neuroendocrine tumours have salt-and-pepper chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli; the two can look alike to the eye.
Pancreatoblastoma adds squamoid nests to the acinar cells and occurs mainly in children.
The solid pseudopapillary neoplasm has poorly cohesive cells round delicate vessels, grooved nuclei and nuclear beta-catenin.
Normal acini sit in orderly lobules with ducts and islets among them; the carcinoma is a mass of acini and sheets.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 895

entries.name: Pancreatoblastoma
entries.line: A childhood tumour: cells with acinar differentiation, with squamoid nests among them.
glance: Cells with acinar differentiation
Squamoid nests scattered among them
entries.remember: Squamoid nests are what separate it from acinar cell carcinoma.

features.architecture: Acinar-type cells with squamoid nests mixed among them.

facts.who: Mainly children aged 1–15; adults rarely. About 0.5% of one centre’s resections. Some with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis.
facts.gross: Fleshy lobules, with fibrosis, necrosis and calcification.
facts.molecular: Trypsin, chymotrypsin and BCL-10 positive; patchy nuclear beta-catenin in some.
facts.outlook: Five-year survival about 65% with resection.

mimics.tell: Acinar cell carcinoma has no squamoid nests and occurs in adults.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 895

entries.name: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm
entries.line: Uniform cells that fall away from one another, leaving sleeves of cells round delicate vessels; mostly in young women.

images.caption: Uniform cells clinging to delicate vessels; the cells between have fallen away (pseudopapillae).
images.credit: Nephron, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: Pink hyaline globules in and between the cells (soft focus).
images.credit: Mikael Häggström, M.D., via Wikimedia Commons

glance: Cuffs of cells round thin vessels (pseudopapillae)
Uniform cells with clear cytoplasm, loosely held together
Oval nuclei with a lengthwise groove
Pink hyaline globules, often
entries.remember: Not a variant of ductal adenocarcinoma: a young woman’s tumour, usually cured by resection.

features.architecture: Solid sheets and pseudopapillae round delicate branching vessels; solid and cystic areas with haemorrhage.
features.cells: Monomorphic, poorly cohesive, clear cytoplasm; hyaline globules often present.

facts.where: Sources differ: equally in head, body and tail, or most often the tail.
facts.who: Mostly girls and young women, median age about 30; 1–2% of pancreatic tumours.
facts.gross: Well demarcated, solid and cystic, with haemorrhagic and necrotic debris.
facts.molecular: CTNNB1 mutation in 83–100%: nuclear beta-catenin; LEF1 and CD10 positive.
facts.outlook: Low malignant potential: most are cured by resection; 10–15% behave aggressively, spreading to liver or peritoneum.

mimics.tell: Neuroendocrine tumours are cohesive nests with salt-and-pepper nuclei; INSM1 marks them, LEF1 and nuclear beta-catenin mark this.
Acinar cell carcinoma has granular cytoplasm and a prominent nucleolus, and stains for trypsin.

sources: Robbins and Cotran 9th ed., ch. 19, p. 891
